q.intro.text: In a quiz game, a wrong answer scores minus three points. You have four points. Then the host finds that one of your wrong answers was right after all, and takes that minus three away.

q.ask.text: Your new score is four minus negative three. What is it?

e.intro.text: Four steps. Press each one: the number line moves first, then the notation.

e.s1.text: Adding negative three would move three to the left: from four to one.

e.s2.text: But the minus three is taken away. Taking it away undoes that move, so the arrow flips: three to the right.

e.s3.text: You land on seven. Four minus negative three is four plus three, which is seven. Taking away a number is adding its opposite.

e.s4.text: Check: add the minus three back. Seven plus negative three is four, the score you started with.

e.why.text: Quick check: why does taking away negative three move to the right?

e.w-ok.text: Yes. Taking away undoes adding. Adding negative three moves left, so taking it away moves right.

e.w-two.text: Two negatives make a positive is a rule for multiplying. In a sum, negative three plus negative four is negative seven, not seven. The reason here is the flip.

e.w-left.text: Then four minus negative three would be one. But losing a penalty can only raise your score: the move is to the right.

t.intro.text: Now you have minus two points, and the host takes away a minus six penalty. Your score is negative two minus negative six. The first step is done for you.

t.s1.text: Adding negative six would move six to the left: from negative two to negative eight.

t.flip.text: Your step. The minus six is taken away. Which way does the arrow point now?

t.f-ok.text: Yes. Taking it away undoes the move, so the arrow flips: six to the right.

t.f-left.text: Subtracting does not always mean left. Taking away negative six undoes a move to the left, and that is a move to the right.

t.land.text: Where does the flipped arrow land? Type the number.

t.l-ok.text: Yes. Negative two minus negative six is negative two plus six, which is four.

t.l-before.text: That is where the arrow pointed before the flip. Taking negative six away flips it: count six to the right of negative two.

t.l-both.text: Only the number taken away changes sign. The negative two stays: negative two plus six.

t.l-other.text: Count six to the right from negative two: two steps reach zero, then four more.

t.check.text: Last step: which addition checks the answer?

t.c-ok.text: Yes. Add the minus six back to four, and you are at negative two again. The answer checks out.

t.c-pair.text: That adds the answer to the first number. Add back the number taken away: four plus negative six is negative two.

t.c-again.text: Doing the same subtraction again can repeat the same slip. Undo it instead: four plus negative six is negative two.

t.cb-right.text: At the start you picked seven, and you were right. Now you can show why: taking away negative three flips the move.

t.cb-one.text: At the start you picked one: that moves left for every minus sign. Taking away negative three flips the move, so four minus negative three is seven.

t.cb-m7.text: At the start you picked negative seven: that adds the sizes and keeps a minus sign. Losing a penalty raises the score: four minus negative three is seven.

t.cb-sure.text: You were sure, and changing your mind after being sure is exactly how this sticks.

p.intro.text: Sam says: subtracting always makes a number smaller.

p.ask.text: Is Sam's claim always true, sometimes true, or never true?

p.j-ok.text: Sometimes. Now prove it: fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.j-test.text: Let's test it. Build the argument and see where it leads.

p.c1.text: Five minus two is three, which is smaller than five,

p.c2.text: but five minus negative two is seven, which is bigger than five,

p.c3.text: so Sam's claim is only sometimes true.

p.x-left.text: That is the idea being tested, and the line disproves it: taking away negative two moves right.

p.x-examples.text: One example that works does not prove a rule for every number. One example that fails does disprove it.

p.x-other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line.

p.done.text: That's a proof: two cases on the number line, and the one that fails settles it. Subtracting makes a number smaller only when the number taken away is positive.
